home.heading: Hi, I'm Erdan!
home.intro: I'm a Product Manager passionate about building products that solve real problems for real people. With experience spanning fintech, healthtech, and marketplace products, I combine analytical thinking with user empathy to drive outcomes that matter.
home.personal: When I am not working you can find me playing soccer, watching documentary films, or building side projects. I enjoy learning how things work and how they can be made better.

Most recently, I worked as a Product Manager Intern at Rae Health, where I defined the company's first North Star metric and supporting metric tree for a live clinical wearable platform.
previousWork: Before graduate school, I spent nearly four years as a Senior IT Project Manager at Attract Group, where I owned the discovery to launch process for 10+ client products across fintech, marketplace, and healthtech, managing cross functional teams of up to 15 engineers and specialists.

On the side, I've been building the PM Thinking Coach. It is a course for people entering product management from zero: two skill trees of 167 skills, 248 lessons, and 36 gates where you decide on a real situation and defend the decision in writing. SwiftUI on iOS, a web client, FastAPI and Postgres behind both.

items.title: PM Thinking Coach
items.summary: A tool for people entering product management from zero. A comprehensive skill map covering both product management and system design, helping you assess your competencies, identify knowledge gaps, and structure your skills. Short lessons explain key concepts, while practical exercises and real-world business simulations help you develop the mindset and problem-solving skills of a product manager.
items.imageAlt: The Skills Map: 71 skill cards arranged in six sectors and three rings, with a red line marking how far the learner has got
items.tagline: The map of the profession, turned into a route you can walk from zero

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: Most material for new product managers is a library: a pile of articles you are trusted to sequence yourself. That works if you already know what you are missing, which is precisely what a beginner does not.

PM Thinking Coach turns the map of the profession into a route. Two skill trees — product management and system design — hold 167 skills between them. Each is a card you can open and read. Each block of skills ends in a gate: a real situation with incomplete data where you decide and defend the decision in writing.
It runs on iOS in SwiftUI and in the browser, both on one FastAPI and Postgres backend, with the same account and the same corpus.
sections.imageAlt: The Learn screen: six directions, the current block, and the next lesson on a black plate
sections.caption: Learn answers two questions and nothing else: which direction am I on, and what do I read next.

sections.heading: A gate, not a quiz
paragraphs: This is the decision the whole product rests on. A multiple-choice test measures whether you remember the right answer; the job measures whether you can defend a call with the evidence you actually have. So a gate hands you a company, a constraint and a deadline, lets you choose what evidence to look at, and then asks you to write down why.

Scoring enforces it rather than merely encouraging it. Rationale and communication carry 60 of 100 points against 25 for the decision itself, and the pass mark is 70 — so picking the option a grader would like, even with every piece of evidence reviewed, cannot pass on its own. A content validator rejects any scenario where a defensible alternative scores too low, which keeps a single-right-answer question out of the corpus by construction.
bullets: Every gate has at least two scenarios, each with a different company, so a retake cannot be passed from memory
Failing costs nothing: no XP is taken, nothing locks, and the result points at the exact lessons that would have helped
The server owns score, XP and unlock status; the client renders them and never derives them, so a UI bug cannot open a gate early
sections.imageAlt: A gate scenario: a shift-scheduling company whose month-two churn has risen from 9% to 16%
sections.caption: A gate opens with a situation, not a question. The evidence you choose to look at is part of what is scored.

sections.heading: The lessons
paragraphs: A lesson is one idea, one model, and where that model stops working — three to five minutes on the product map, twelve to fifteen in system design. Every domain follows one fictional company through all of its blocks, so the examples accumulate instead of resetting.

Lessons can carry an audio overview: two hosts talking the lesson through, in the sense NotebookLM made familiar. It is deliberately not the lesson read aloud — prose read out loud always sounds like prose read out loud. The dialogue is written once at build time and stored as a content file, so it can be reviewed and edited like any other, and the runtime never calls a model.

The model that writes it is checked, not trusted: a draft is rejected if it uses a number or a term that does not appear in the lesson, if it collapses into a monologue, or if it quotes the lesson verbatim. Edit the lesson and its overview stops counting as current rather than quietly voicing last week's edition.
sections.imageAlt: A lesson page with its audio overview player and a summary card headed “The point”
sections.caption: A lesson, its audio overview, and the one thing to take away from it.

sections.heading: What is in it
paragraphs: The corpus is authored, not generated — and it is finished. Both trees are fully published.
bullets: Two skill trees: product management (18 blocks, 71 skills) and system design (18 blocks, 96 skills), each open from day one
248 lessons, 36 gates and 87 gate scenarios, every one written and reviewed
96 exercises in system design that are formative on purpose: no XP, no effect on what opens next, and the reference reasoning comes back even on an empty submission
A 489-term glossary, and diagrams stored as structure rather than pictures, so a screen reader gets a description rather than an image
Eight competencies tracked per learner, one per domain of the map plus communication and system design

Bilingual: Russian is the authored source, English is an overlay merged over it. The rubric and option weights exist in one copy only, so the language someone reads in cannot change what they score — a property of the construction, not of discipline
sections.imageAlt: The Progress screen: level, XP, blocks passed, lessons read, and the eight competencies
sections.caption: Progress owns the numbers, so the other screens do not repeat them.

sections.heading: Where it stands
paragraphs: Both trees are complete and a full traversal has been verified end to end through the API. The evaluator currently runs a deterministic mock: it exercises the whole flow, but the coaching text reads as a stub and gate calibration against the QA fixtures is not meaningful until a real provider is wired up. That is the next decision, and it is deliberately the last one — nothing about the product depends on which model answers.
bullets: Defined the beta success metrics before launch: activation, time to first value, D7 repeat practice, and whether the feedback was useful

items.caption: The skill map, made interactive. The red frontier is the only colour on it — it marks exactly what you have covered.

items.title: Rae Health
items.meta: Product Manager Intern; Bristol, ME. June 2026 - September 2026
items.summary: Defined the first North Star metric and metric tree for a live clinical wearable platform, and pressure-tested the ROI model behind the growth strategy.
items.tagline: Giving a clinical wearable platform its first real baseline

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Worked on a live clinical wearable platform, defining foundational product metrics and validating growth strategy through data analysis and customer research.

sections.heading: What RAE is
paragraphs: RAE stands for Realize, Analyze, Engage. It is a wearable and an app for people in recovery from substance use disorder: the band reads physiology continuously, models pick out the signature of stress or a craving, and the app offers a way to de-escalate at the moment it happens rather than at the next appointment.

The product is built for three audiences at once — people in recovery, the treatment providers and care teams supporting them, and employers running wellness programmes. The company is supported by the National Institutes of Health and UT Tyler, runs a study with UMass Medical School and Garmin, and holds two US patents.
sections.imageAlt: The RAE Health site, showing the tagline “Realize. Analyze. Engage.” and the wearable band
sections.caption: Realize, Analyze, Engage — and the band that does the reading.

sections.heading: How the detection works
paragraphs: The wearable measures accelerometry, skin conductance, skin temperature and heart rate. Machine learning over those signals identifies biomarkers of stress and craving. When one fires, the device vibrates and the app opens de-escalation tools — breathing exercises among them — so the response lands while the state is still happening.
Nothing is left to the sensor alone: a patient can log an event by hand, which both fills the gaps and gives the models something to be checked against.
sections.imageAlt: The RAE app capturing a stress event step by step, next to a calendar of event trends
sections.caption: Capturing an event, and the trends it feeds.

sections.heading: What the published research says
paragraphs: The detection has been evaluated in peer-reviewed work: the model identified stress correctly 76% of the time and craving 69%, with false positive rates of 33% and 28%. Clients reported heightened awareness of their own patterns; providers saw an opening for more personalised care.

That is the context the metrics work sat in. A product whose value rests on detection being trustworthy enough to act on needs to know how many patients are actually active, how dense the monitoring really is, and how often anyone responds — which is what the baseline below set out to establish.

sections.heading: What I did
bullets: Defined the company's first North Star metric and supporting metric tree (Reach → Activation → Retention → Clinical Engagement)
Analyzed event-level data (85 patients, ~91,000 detection events, 6 months) to compute the product's first measured baseline

Stress-tested the ROI model behind the company's growth strategy: traced each figure to source, formula, or "unverifiable", then recomputed break-even and reframed the claim before it reached prospects
Ran 6 customer interviews alongside usability studies to validate hypotheses before committing engineering capacity, and turned a gap in the acquisition funnel into a scoped backlog item
sections.imageAlt: The RAE app showing stress event intensity and event counts broken down by time of day
sections.caption: The analytics the baseline came out of: event intensity and counts by time of day.

items.tagline: Two client engagements, from stakeholder interviews to shipped tooling

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Questrom Consulting Lab pairs graduate teams with companies on real problems on a fixed timeline. I ran two engagements, both with technology clients, covering stakeholder discovery, scoping, delivery and the hand-off at the end.

sections.heading: LinkSquares — mapping the back office
paragraphs: LinkSquares is a Boston company building AI-powered contract lifecycle management software, founded in 2015 and used by more than 1,200 customers including DraftKings, Wayfair and TIME. It has raised roughly $164M, including a $100M Series C in 2022.
Fast growth leaves a company buying tools faster than it retires them. The engagement was to find out what the business actually runs on, and where the same job was being paid for twice.
bullets: Mapped 150+ back-office systems across 9 departments through 8 stakeholder interviews
Built a systems-relationship tool that surfaced $700K in projected annual savings from redundant tooling
sections.imageAlt: The LinkSquares site, showing its contract management platform and customer logos
sections.caption: LinkSquares sells contract lifecycle management to legal teams at companies like DraftKings, TIME and Wayfair.

sections.heading: Sikich — an enterprise AI knowledge assistant
paragraphs: Sikich is a Chicago-based professional services firm founded in 1982, offering accounting, advisory, technology and managed services, and ranked 27th on Accounting Today's Top 100 firms.

A firm that size holds most of its expertise in documents and in people's heads. The engagement was to make that knowledge answerable — a retrieval-augmented assistant staff could ask directly, rather than a search box over a file share.
bullets: Led development of the enterprise AI knowledge assistant and its RAG solution
Coordinated project execution, technical workstreams, deliverables and stakeholder alignment across the engagement
sections.imageAlt: The Sikich site, with the headline “Turn complex challenges into simple solutions”
sections.caption: Sikich: accounting, advisory, technology and managed services, from Chicago.

sections.heading: Projects I led
paragraphs: Here are some of the 10+ products I ran at Attract Group

sections.heading: Rae Health — stress and craving management on wearables
paragraphs: A healthcare platform that pairs patented biomarker wearables with mobile apps and a clinical web portal, so patients can see what triggers a craving and clinicians can adjust treatment on real data. The largest engagement I ran: 24+ months and a $200,000+ budget.
bullets: Automatic detection of stress and craving events from wearable biomarkers, with manual entry so nothing goes unrecorded
Calendar and statistics views that turn individual events into patterns a clinician can act on
RAE Connect for caregivers and support networks, and a web clinical portal for reviewing patient data and tuning care plans
Flutter and the Garmin SDK on mobile; Java, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL and AWS behind it
sections.imageAlt: The RAE Connect clinical portal showing stress and craving calendars, beside the patient app
sections.caption: The clinical portal: stress and craving events laid out as calendars a clinician can read at a glance.

sections.heading: Wild Atlantic Health — home testing and supplement commerce
paragraphs: An Irish platform that closes the loop from a home blood test to the supplement that answers it: activate a kit, send the sample, get doctor-reviewed results, and buy what the results recommend. Six months, $80,000+.
bullets: Third-party laboratory integration returning doctor-reviewed vitamin D and omega-3 insights within 7 working days
A recommendation flow tying each test result to specific products, rather than a generic catalogue
Stripe checkout, delivery tracking and reviews, with an admin panel for orders and content
Laravel on the backend, React on the frontend, Flutter on mobile
sections.imageAlt: The Wild Atlantic Health store, showing a vitamin D product page on desktop and mobile
sections.caption: The store side of the platform, where a test result turns into a specific recommendation.

sections.heading: Curbside Kitchen — a marketplace for food trucks
paragraphs: Office cafeterias are expensive to run. Curbside Kitchen lets property managers book food trucks instead, and gives truck owners a steady stream of bookings. A role-based marketplace for property owners, truck owners, office workers and administrators. Eleven months, $50,000–$100,000.
bullets: A scheduler and event management flow that matches requests to suitable trucks without manual back-and-forth
Stripe payments and invoicing, plus disputes, auto-refunds and rating management
SMS and email campaigns through Twilio, Mailgun and ActiveCampaign; Google and Apple Calendar sync
Reached 2,000+ completed events, 400+ more planned, 200 registered trucks and around 100 properties
Django and PostgreSQL

bullets: Rebuilt the customer account: purchase history, document downloads, and planning upgrades to a kit already owned
Currency conversion for international buyers, automated invoicing, and order export for operations
Organisation purchases for business customers, and Google Analytics instrumentation to steer the work
WordPress and WooCommerce
